You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 0.76 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal (weak); Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 6800 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 22000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weakest excitation; Ip = 8 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 22000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 10 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:

S3       2.24    2.26    35.4   0.329     0.228  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S4      0.334   0.339    8.95       -   0.00508  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok

S6      0.459   0.462     6.1       -    0.0211  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 5 of 12.

RESULTS OF YOUR PREVIOUS ROUND:

what this means:
- with the output fixed at 1.8 V, the net power delivered covers only -189 % of the load's need on S2 (heavy load), -613 % of the load's need on S4 (weakest excitation), -280 % of the load's need on S6 (Cp +20 %, hot) (best of the value presets tried)

REPEATED PROBLEM: your last three designs all show the same failure: too little power reaches the output on some conditions [underpower]. Change the part of the circuit responsible for it rather than its values.

reply.reasoning:
*   Piezo source: Sinusoidal current $I_p \sin(2\pi ft)$ in parallel with $C_p$ (25-30nF) and 20M$\Omega$ leakage.
    *   Open-circuit voltage $V_{oc} = I_p / (2\pi f C_p) \approx 0.76$ V.
    *   Target Output $V_{out}$: 1.8 V to 3.6 V.
    *   Load $R_L$: 6.8 M$\Omega$ to 22 M$\Omega$.
    *   Required: Cold start to 1.8 V in 0.4 s, low ripple (50 mV), settled output.

    *   The $V_{oc}$ (0.76 V) is significantly lower than the target $V_{out}$ (1.8 V).
    *   This means a standard rectifier (like FBR) will never work unless $I_p$ is very high (S3) or the voltage is boosted.
    *   Passive rectification (FBR) fails because the diodes only conduct when $|V_{pzp}| > V_{out} + V_{diode}$. With $V_{out} = 1.8$ V and $V_{oc} \approx 0.76$ V, a simple bridge cannot pump charge into the capacitor once it reaches $\approx 0.5$ V (since $V_{oc} \approx 0.76$ and diode drop $\approx 0.25$).
    *   We need a DC-DC boost mechanism.

    *   P-SSHI (Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor) is designed to flip the voltage across $C_p$ at the peaks to increase the extracted energy.
    *   However, the previous implementation [c0034] failed miserably ($V_{out} < 0.22$ V).
    *   Looking at [c0034] topology:
        `D1 D pzp out DSCH`
        `D2 D pzn out DSCH`
        `D3 D 0 pzp DSCH`
        `D4 D 0 pzn DSCH`
        `L1 L pzp n1 0.000917`
        `S1 S n1 pzn ctrl=G1`
        `G1 SYNC ton=1.23e-05s phase=0.17 edges=both`
        `C1 C out 0 4.7e-05`
        `DZ1 D 0 out DZ33`
    *   The problem here is that the diodes D1-D4 form a bridge, but the L-S circuit is connected to `pzp` and `pzn`. The L-S circuit tries to flip the voltage, but the bridge is likely clamping the voltage or fighting the flipping process. Specifically, the bridge will conduct whenever the voltage exceeds the diode drops, potentially preventing the voltage from building up to the level needed for the inductor to effectively transfer energy or for the diodes to push it to $V_{out}$ if $V_{out} > V_{oc}$.

    *   Standard SSHI usually involves a switch (or inductor-switch) to flip $V_{Cp}$ and a rectifier to move charge to $C_{out}$.
    *   To get $V_{out} > V_{oc}$, we need a boost-like action.
    *   A classic SSHI circuit:
        1.  $C_p$ charges up.
        2.  At peak, a switch closes across $L$, flipping the charge on $C_p$ ($\approx -V_{peak}$).
        3.  The voltage then climbs from $-V_{peak}$ to $+V_{peak}$ (or vice versa), and the rectifier harvests this.
    *   But wait: the total voltage swing is $2 V_{peak}$. If $V_{peak} \approx 0.76$ V, the swing is 1.52 V. Even with this, if we use a bridge, we are still limited by the peak voltage.
    *   Actually, SSHI works by making $V_{Cp}$ a square-ish wave, but the *peak* voltage across $C_p$ can be higher than $V_{oc}$.
    *   Let's consider a "Boost-Rectifier" where the inductor is used as a boost inductor.
    *   But $V_{oc}$ is very low. We need a way to build up voltage.

    *   The "Balanced-Boost" failed screening.
    *   Let's try a simpler, more robust Boost topology.
    *   If we use a synchronous switch to create a boost converter:
        Piezo $\rightarrow$ Inductor $\rightarrow$ Switch to GND $\rightarrow$ Diode to Out.
    *   Wait, the piezo is a current source. If we short it via an inductor and switch, we can build up energy in the inductor and then kick it up to $V_{out}$.
    *   Circuit:
        Piezo nodes: pzp, pzn.
        L1: pzp to n1.
        S1: n1 to 0 (controlled by G1).
        D1: n1 to out.
        C1: out to 0.
        This is a boost converter. Since the piezo is AC, we need this to work for both half-cycles.

    *   A full-wave boost:
        Cycle 1 (positive):
        L1: pzp to n1.
        S1: n1 to 0.
        D1: n1 to out.
        Cycle 2 (negative):
        L2: pzn to n2.
        S2: n2 to 0.
        D2: n2 to out.
        G1: edges=both, ton=...
    *   Wait, the current $I_p$ is sinusoidal. In the first half cycle ($I_p > 0$), current flows from pzp to pzn.
    *   If we have L1 from pzp to n1, and S1 from n1 to 0, the current $I_p$ charges L1. When S1 opens, the energy in L1 is pushed through D1 to $V_{out}$.
    *   Similarly for the second half cycle using pzn, L2, S2, and D2.

    *   $V_{oc} \approx 0.76$ V. This is the *amplitude* of the voltage across $C_p$ if it were open.
    *   If we short $C_p$ (via L and S), we are essentially harvesting the current $I_p$.
    *   Energy per half-cycle $\approx \int I_p^2 \frac{L}{2}$? No, the inductor is charged by the current source.
    *   Actually, if we close the switch, the current $I_p$ flows through the inductor. The inductor current $I_L$ becomes $\int I_p dt$.
    *   $I_{L,peak} = \int_0^{T/2} I_p \sin(2\pi f t) dt = \frac{I_p}{\pi f}$.
    *   For $I_p = 12\mu$A, $f=100$Hz, $I_{L,peak} = \frac{12\mu\text{A}}{100\pi} \approx 38\text{ nA}$.
    *   This is incredibly small. The energy $1/2 L I_L^2$ would be negligible.
    *   Wait, I'm miscalculating. The piezo is not just a current source; it's a current source in parallel with $C_p$.
    *   The energy available is mainly in $C_p$. $E = 1/2 C_p V_{oc}^2$.
    *   $E = 0.5 \times 25\text{nF} \times (0.76\text{V})^2 \approx 7.2\text{ nJ}$ per half-cycle.
    *   Total power $\approx 2 \times E \times f = 2 \times 7.2\text{nJ} \times 100\text{Hz} = 1.44\mu\text{W}$.
    *   The load $R_L$ is $10\text{M}\Omega$ at 1.8 V $\rightarrow P = V^2/R = 1.8^2 / 10^7 = 3.24 \times 10^{-7} / 10 = 0.324\mu\text{W}$.
    *   So the power is there, but we must extract it efficiently.

    *   SSHI works by flipping the voltage on $C_p$ so that it doesn't just oscillate around 0, but instead stays biased, effectively increasing the voltage difference across the rectifier.
    *   If $V_{Cp}$ is flipped from $+V_{peak}$ to $-V_{peak}$, then in the next half cycle it goes from $-V_{peak}$ to $+V_{peak}$, the total swing is $2 V_{peak}$.
    *   The ideal SSHI voltage across $C_p$ becomes a square wave with amplitude $V_{peak} / (1 - \text{efficiency})$.
    *   Wait, the crucial part of SSHI is the "flipping" switch.
    *   Standard SSHI:
        1.  Piezo $C_p$ is in parallel with the source.
        2.  An inductor $L$ and switch $S$ are in parallel with $C_p$.
        3.  When $V_{Cp}$ reaches a peak, $S$ closes for $t_{on} \approx \pi\sqrt{LC_p}$, flipping $V_{Cp}$.
        4.  The rectifier (usually a diode or synchronous) then extracts charge.

    *   Let's try a simpler SSHI with a diode rectifier:
        - $C_p$ is between pzp and pzn.
        - $L1$ between pzp and n1.
        - $S1$ between n1 and pzn.
        - $G1$ (SYNC) controls $S1$ at both edges.
        - To extract the energy: a diode $D1$ from pzp to $out$, and $D2$ from pzn to $out$.
        - Wait, if $D1$ is from pzp to $out$, then $V_{pzp}$ must be $> V_{out}$.
        - But $V_{pzp}$ only reaches $V_{peak}$ (0.76V) without SSHI. With SSHI, $V_{pzp}$ can reach higher values, but it's still limited.
        - Actually, the SSHI voltage is $V_{out}$ *if* the rectifier is a diode. The charge is pushed to $V_{out}$.
        - But the diode $D1$ (pzp to $out$) will only conduct if $V_{pzp} > V_{out}$.
        - In SSHI, the flipping happens *at* the peak. The voltage then rises.
        - If $V_{out} = 1.8$ V and $V_{oc} = 0.76$ V, we need the flipping to happen and the resulting voltage to exceed 1.8 V.
        - This only happens if $V_{pzp}$ is already high.
        - How does it start? Cold start.
        - At cold start, $V_{out} = 0$. $V_{pzp}$ will reach $V_{oc} = 0.76$ V. The diode $D1$ will conduct, charging $V_{out}$ to $\approx 0.76 - 0.25 = 0.51$ V.
        - Now $V_{out} = 0.51$ V. The diode $D1$ only conducts if $V_{pzp} > 0.76$ V.
        - But the piezo only provides $0.76$ V. It will never reach 1.8 V.

    *   Wait! If the SSHI flipping is working, the voltage across $C_p$ doesn't just stay at $V_{oc}$. The flipping prevents the current source from "seeing" the capacitor charge, effectively allowing $V_{Cp}$ to build up.
    *   Actually, the SSHI voltage $V_{Cp}$ settles to $V_{out} + V_{diode}$.
    *   Let's try the most basic SSHI:
        - $L1$ between pzp and n1.
        - $S1$ between n1 and pzn.
        - $G1$ (SYNC) controls $S1$, `edges="both"`, `ton` $\approx \pi\sqrt{LC_p}$.
        - $D1$ from pzp to $out$.
        - $D2$ from pzn to $out$.
        - Wait, this is for a piezo that is grounded at one end. Our piezo is pzp and pzn.
        - If we use a bridge:
            - $D1$ pzp to $out$
            - $D2$ pzn to $out$
            - $D3$ 0 to pzp
            - $D4$ 0 to pzn
            - This is the bridge from the P-SSHI [c0034]. Why did it fail?
            - In [c0034], the inductor $L1$ was between pzp and n1, and $S1$ between n1 and pzn.
            - The bridge was $D1(pzp, out), D2(pzn, out), D3(0, pzp), D4(0, pzn)$.
            - The problem is that the bridge clamps $V_{pzp}$ and $V_{pzn}$ to $[ -V_{out}, V_{out} ]$.
            - If $V_{out} = 1.8$ V, then $V_{pzp}$ can never exceed 1.8 V, and $V_{pzn}$ can never be less than -1.8 V.
            - But SSHI *needs* $V_{pzp}$ to reach a peak, flip, and then rise.
            - If the bridge is always there, the flipping is hindered.
            - Wait, the SSHI flip happens *at* the peak. If the bridge is there, the peak is clamped.
            - Actually, the standard SSHI uses a *single* diode (or a synchronous rectifier) and a capacitor.
            - Let's try a "half-bridge" SSHI:
                - Piezo: pzp, pzn.
                - $L1$ between pzp and n1.
                - $S1$ between n1 and pzn.
                - $G1$ (SYNC) controls $S1$, `edges="both"`.
                - $D1$ from pzp to $out$.
                - $D2$ from pzn to $out$. (Wait, this would only work if pzn is the "return" path).
                - Let's make pzn the reference for the flipping:
                    - $L1$ from pzp to n1.
                    - $S1$ from n1 to pzn.
                    - $G1$ controls $S1$.
                    - Then we need a way to get charge from both pzp and pzn to $out$.
                    - If $S1$ flips the voltage across $C_p$, then $V_{pzp}$ will oscillate between some $V_{high}$ and $V_{low}$ relative to $V_{pzn}$.
                    - This is getting confusing. Let's try a simpler approach.

    *   A boost converter that takes the AC from the piezo.
    *   Half-wave boost:
        - $L1$: pzp to n1.
        - $S1$: n1 to 0.
        - $D1$: n1 to out.
        - $G1$ (SYNC): `edges="pos"`, `ton` = something small.
        - This takes only the positive half-cycle.
    *   Full-wave boost:
        - $L1$: pzp to n1.
        - $S1$: n1 to 0.
        - $D1$: n1 to out.
        - $L2$: pzn to n2.
        - $S2$: n2 to 0.
        - $D2$: n2 to out.
        - $G1$ (SYNC): `edges="both"`, `ton` = something small.
        - When $G1$ is on, $S1$ and $S2$ are closed.
        - This means in the positive half-cycle, current flows $pzp \rightarrow L1 \rightarrow S1 \rightarrow 0$.
        - In the negative half-cycle, current flows $pzn \rightarrow L2 \rightarrow S2 \rightarrow 0$.
        - When $S1, S2$ open, the inductors kick the charge to $V_{out}$.
        - But wait: the current is $I_p \sin(\omega t)$.
        - For the positive half-cycle, $I_p$ is from pzp to pzn.
        - So current flows $pzp \rightarrow L1 \rightarrow S1 \rightarrow 0$.
        - Then it must return $0 \rightarrow pzn$.
        - Since the piezo is a current source, the return path is automatic.
        - This is just two boost converters in parallel.

    *   $I_p = 12\mu$A. $L = 1$mH.
    *   $t_{on} = 1\text{ms}$ (too long, the peak is at $T/4 = 2.5\text{ms}$).
    *   Wait, if we just use the SYNC at the peaks:
        - $G1$ `edges="both"`, `ton` = 1ms.
        - This will close $S1, S2$ at the peaks of $V_{pzp}$.
        - At the peak, the inductor current is zero? No, the current source $I_p \sin(\omega t)$ is zero at the peaks of $V_{pzp}$.
        - $V_{pzp}$ peaks when $I_p$ is zero.
        - If we close the switch at the voltage peak, we are flipping the charge on $C_p$ using $L$.
        - This is exactly what SSHI does!
        - So:
            - $L1$: pzp to n1.
            - $S1$: n1 to pzn. (Flip across the piezo)
            - $G1$: `edges="both"`, `ton` = $\pi\sqrt{LC_p}$.
            - Now we have a voltage swing. How to extract it?
            - With $V_{out} = 1.8$ V and $V_{oc} = 0.76$ V, a simple diode $D1(pzp, out)$ will only work if the flipping boosts $V_{pzp}$ above 2.05 V.
            - Can SSHI boost the voltage that high?
            - In theory, yes. The voltage $V_{Cp}$ can increase until it's limited by the load or a zener.
